paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, bamboo was regarded in the industrialised world as a material for garden furniture and fishing rods rather than for serious construction. Yet across Asia, Latin America and Africa, more than a billion people live in houses that depend on it, and engineers are now taking a second look at a plant that grows faster than any tree. Shoots of moso, a giant species native to China, have been recorded adding almost a metre to their height in a single day. A stand of moso can be harvested after only four or five years, whereas most softwood plantations need thirty years or more before the timber is ready to cut. Because the plant regrows from an extensive underground root system, harvesting does not require replanting, and the soil is not left bare.

Botanically, bamboo is not a tree at all but a giant grass. Its stems, known as culms, are hollow tubes divided at regular intervals by solid internal partitions, which appear on the outside as raised rings called nodes. This design gives the culm great stiffness for very little weight, on the same principle that makes a steel tube harder to bend than a solid rod of equal mass. The strength itself comes from long fibres running the length of the stem. These are not spread uniformly through the wall: they are packed most densely towards the outer surface, where bending forces are greatest, and become sparser towards the hollow interior. Tested along the grain, the fibres of some species have a tensile strength comparable to that of mild steel, which has led enthusiasts to call bamboo 'vegetable steel'.

Builders in earthquake zones have long understood the advantages of such a material. At the end of the 1990s, when a powerful earthquake struck the coffee-growing region of western Colombia, many of the traditional houses known as bahareque, which have a bamboo frame covered with a mixture of mud and plaster, remained standing while more modern brick and concrete buildings nearby collapsed. Engineers attribute this to two properties. A bamboo frame is light, so the forces generated by shaking are relatively small, and it is flexible enough to bend and then recover rather than crack.

Despite these qualities, bamboo has three weaknesses that have kept it out of mainstream construction. The first is its vulnerability to insects and fungi. The culm stores large amounts of starch, which makes it an attractive food for beetles, and untreated bamboo exposed to rain and sun may last as little as two years. The second problem is irregularity. No two culms are identical, and even within a single stem the diameter and wall thickness change from base to tip, so engineers find it difficult to calculate with confidence how much load a structure will bear. Finally, bamboo is awkward to join. Nails, the standard fastening of timber construction, tend to split the culm along its fibres, and the round, hollow shape offers few flat surfaces to connect.

Each of these problems now has at least a partial solution. The most widely used treatment involves soaking freshly cut culms in a solution of borax and boric acid, which replaces the starch and makes the bamboo unappetising to insects. The chemicals are cheap and of low toxicity, and properly treated bamboo kept dry can last for twenty-five years or more. In some villages a traditional alternative is still practised: culms are left in running water for several weeks so that the starch is gradually washed out. To solve the problem of joining, builders in Colombia developed a technique in which the hollow segments at the end of each culm are filled with mortar, a mixture of cement, sand and water, and the pieces are then fastened with steel bolts that pass through the solid core.

The irregularity of natural culms has proved the hardest problem, and here the most promising response is engineered bamboo. Culms are split into thin strips, or crushed into mats of fibre, which are then dried, coated with adhesive and pressed under heat into boards and beams of standard dimensions. One such product, known as strand-woven bamboo, is denser than most hardwoods and is already widely sold as flooring. At the University of Westbrook, a research group led by the structural engineer Dr Helen Marsh has tested laminated bamboo beams and found that their strength varies far less from one sample to the next than that of natural culms, which allows them to be designed using the same methods as timber. Critics point out, however, that the adhesives used are often based on chemicals derived from oil, and that drying and pressing consume considerable energy, so that some of the plant's environmental advantage is lost in the factory.

Supporters also stress bamboo's value in the fight against climate change. Because it grows so rapidly, a managed bamboo forest absorbs carbon dioxide quickly, and as long as the harvested culms end up in long-lasting buildings rather than being burned or left to rot, that carbon remains locked away. Whether bamboo will move from the margins to the mainstream, though, depends less on the plant than on people. Only a handful of countries have building codes covering bamboo structures, international design standards have appeared only recently, and most architects have never been trained to use it. Until that changes, the world's fastest-growing building material is likely to remain one of its least used.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Between three and six kilometres beneath the surface of the Pacific Ocean, scattered across the abyssal plains between Hawaii and Mexico, lie billions of tonnes of dark, potato-sized lumps known as polymetallic nodules. Each has formed as metals dissolved in seawater slowly built up in layers around a core such as a fragment of shell or a shark's tooth. The process is extraordinarily slow: a typical nodule grows by just a few millimetres every million years. The area where they are most abundant, the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, covers some 4.5 million square kilometres, and the nodules lying on its floor are thought to contain more nickel, cobalt and manganese than all known reserves on land.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: What has changed is the demand for the metals they contain. Nickel, cobalt and manganese are key ingredients in the batteries that power electric vehicles and store electricity from wind and solar farms, and mining companies argue that the seabed offers a less damaging source than the land. Reaching a seam of nickel ore on land commonly means stripping away forest and topsoil, after which the ore must be blasted out of solid rock. Nodules, by contrast, sit loose on the surface of the seabed, so nothing needs to be dug or blasted. And because each nodule is unusually rich in metal, supporters claim, far less waste is left over after processing than with ores mined on land.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The proposed method of collection resembles an underwater version of harvesting a field. A remotely operated vehicle about the size of a combine harvester crawls across the seabed on caterpillar tracks, using jets of water to lift the nodules, together with the top few centimetres of sediment, into its body. There the nodules are separated from most of the mud and pumped up a riser pipe several kilometres long to a ship on the surface, where they are stored before being taken ashore. The water and fine sediment removed on board are then discharged back into the ocean. In a trial in 2022, one company's prototype brought more than 3,000 tonnes of nodules to the surface, demonstrating that the engineering, at least, is feasible.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Biologists, however, warn that the abyssal plain is not the lifeless desert it was once assumed to be. Recent surveys of the Clarion-Clipperton Zone have recorded more than 5,000 species, the great majority of them previously unknown to science. Many are tiny worms and crustaceans living in the sediment, but others, including certain sponges and soft corals, can survive only by attaching themselves to the nodules, which provide the sole hard surface in a landscape of soft mud. Removing the nodules therefore means removing the habitat itself, and on any timescale relevant to human beings it will not return.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: How quickly the seabed might recover from disturbance is difficult to establish, because so few long-term studies exist. The most informative began in 1989, when German scientists dragged a plough-like device repeatedly across eleven square kilometres of seabed off the coast of Peru to imitate the effects of mining. When a team led by the marine ecologist Dr Antje Brenner returned to the site twenty-six years later, the tracks were still clearly visible, and the numbers of many animal groups remained well below those in undisturbed areas nearby. If a modest experiment could leave a mark lasting decades, commercial mining, which would affect hundreds of square kilometres each year, may cause damage that is effectively permanent.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The effects would not be confined to the strips of seabed actually mined. As the collectors move, they stir up clouds of fine particles, known as plumes, and further plumes are created when waste water is released from the surface ship. Depending on currents, these may drift for tens or even hundreds of kilometres before settling, potentially smothering filter-feeding animals far from the mining site. In 2024 an additional concern was raised when a study suggested that nodules might produce oxygen on the deep seabed through a weak electrical charge on their surfaces, implying that removing them could affect the supply of oxygen to deep-sea life. Other scientists, including some funded by mining companies, have strongly disputed the result, and the question remains open.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Responsibility for the seabed beyond national borders lies with the International Seabed Authority (ISA), a body established in 1994 under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. The ISA has issued more than thirty contracts allowing companies and governments to explore the seabed, but after more than a decade of negotiation it has still not agreed on the rules that would govern commercial extraction. Its position is an uncomfortable one, since it is charged both with protecting the marine environment and with organising the exploitation of seabed minerals for the benefit of humankind. Meanwhile, more than thirty countries have called for a pause in deep-sea mining, and several large car manufacturers and technology firms have promised not to use metals from the seabed until its environmental effects are better understood.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Even on purely economic grounds, the case for deep-sea mining is less certain than its advocates suggest. Battery chemistry is changing rapidly: lithium iron phosphate batteries, which contain neither nickel nor cobalt, already power a large and growing share of the world's electric cars. Improved recycling of old batteries could further reduce the need for newly mined metals, and the price of nickel fell sharply after 2022 as new supplies arrived from mines on land. The question facing the world, then, may not be whether the metals on the ocean floor can be collected, but whether they are needed badly enough to justify the risks.

passages.title: Does the language we speak shape how we think?

paragraphs.text: In the 1930s Benjamin Lee Whorf, a fire-prevention inspector with an amateur passion for linguistics, put forward an idea that has never quite gone away. Having studied Hopi, a language of the American south-west, he argued that its speakers understood time in a fundamentally different way from speakers of English, because Hopi grammar did not treat time as a series of countable units. The strong version of this claim, that we can think only what our language allows us to say, now has very few defenders. But a weaker version, that the language we speak habitually steers our attention and memory in particular directions, has enjoyed a remarkable revival, and I believe it deserves more serious consideration than its critics are willing to give it.

Whorf's own evidence did not survive scrutiny. Later fieldwork showed that Hopi has a rich vocabulary for talking about time, and it emerged that Whorf had relied heavily on a single Hopi speaker living in New York. By the 1960s, the intellectual climate had turned against him. Linguists increasingly emphasised the features that all human languages share, and an influential survey of colour words published in 1969 concluded that, although languages differ in how many basic colour terms they have, these terms are added in a remarkably predictable order. Linguistic relativity was quietly dismissed as a romantic error. In my view this was an overreaction: Whorf had asked a reasonable question, and the weakness of his answer was no reason to stop asking it.

The question was revived by research on colour. Russian, unlike English, has no single everyday word for 'blue'; instead it obliges speakers to choose between goluboy, for lighter shades, and siniy, for darker ones. The psychologist Elena Varga showed Russian and English speakers three squares of blue and asked them to say, as quickly as possible, which of the bottom two matched the top one. Russian speakers were faster when the two shades fell on opposite sides of the goluboy-siniy boundary; English speakers showed no such advantage. Crucially, the effect disappeared when participants were asked to silently repeat a string of digits during the task, which occupies the mental resources used for language. The difference amounted to only around a tenth of a second, but its disappearance under verbal interference suggests that language was involved in the act of perception itself, not merely in describing it afterwards.

Evidence from spatial language is, to my mind, more striking still. Speakers of Guugu Yimithirr, an Aboriginal language of northern Australia, do not use words for 'left' and 'right' to describe the positions of objects; instead they use compass directions. Researchers led by the anthropologist David Okafor asked Guugu Yimithirr and Dutch speakers to memorise a row of objects on a table, then turned them around to face a second table and asked them to recreate the arrangement. Dutch speakers preserved the order relative to their own bodies, whereas Guugu Yimithirr speakers preserved its compass orientation. Sceptics such as the psychologist Martin Hale have objected that the two groups differ in more than language: one lives largely in open rural country, the other in towns, and when English speakers are tested outdoors with clear landmarks they too begin to use compass-based directions. This is a fair point, but it does not explain why speakers of different languages living in the same environment often perform the task differently.

Other findings have fared less well. One widely reported study claimed that grammatical gender affects how people think about objects: German speakers, for whom the word for 'bridge' is feminine, supposedly described bridges as 'elegant', while Spanish speakers, for whom it is masculine, chose words such as 'strong'. The result appeared in countless magazine articles and popular books, yet when other laboratories attempted to repeat the experiments with larger samples, they found no consistent effect. Admittedly, the field has at times been harmed by its own enthusiasm, and small, eye-catching studies have too often been treated as conclusive. Popular accounts have made matters worse with headlines claiming that speakers of a particular language 'cannot see' a colour or 'have no sense of' the future, claims that the original researchers rarely made.

The most dramatic evidence comes from the Pirahã, a small community in the Amazon whose language appears to lack words for exact numbers, having only terms roughly meaning 'few' and 'many'. When asked to match a row of objects with the same number of objects of their own, Pirahã speakers performed well with two or three items but made increasing errors with larger quantities. This might seem to confirm the strong version of Whorf's hypothesis. Yet I am cautious about drawing that conclusion, because the Pirahã also have a culture in which exact counting plays almost no role in daily life. With a single community, there is no way to determine whether it is the absence of number words or the absence of any need to count that explains their performance.

What, then, can reasonably be concluded? The effects of language on thought are real, but they are typically modest, and they tend to appear in tasks that require rapid responses; when people are given time to reflect, the differences between speakers of different languages often shrink or vanish. Language, in other words, seems to act less like a prison than like a default setting, one that shapes what we notice first but that can be overridden. The most promising research now concerns bilingual speakers, whose behaviour in some experiments shifts depending on which language they are using. Because the comparison is made within the same individuals, whose culture and environment stay constant, such studies avoid the problem that has haunted the field since Whorf.

3.why: 'vary from the base to the tip' = 'change from base to tip'; đi cùng 'diameter' là 'wall thickness'.

4.why: Engineered bamboo: ép thành 'boards and beams of standard dimensions' nên điền 'dimensions'.

5.why: 'tend to split the culm' giữ nguyên; chủ ngữ là 'Nails'.

6.why: 'hollow end segments filled with' = 'hollow segments at the end of each culm are filled with mortar'. 'cement' chỉ là thành phần của mortar, không phải thứ được nhồi vào.

7.quote: A stand of moso can be harvested after only four or five years, whereas most softwood plantations need thirty years or more
7.why: 4–5 năm so với 30 năm trở lên của rừng gỗ mềm = 'much sooner than most softwood trees'. Khớp nên TRUE.

8.quote: Botanically, bamboo is not a tree at all but a giant grass.
8.why: Về mặt thực vật học tre 'không phải cây gỗ mà là cỏ khổng lồ', trái ngược 'classify bamboo as a type of tree' nên FALSE.

9.quote: These are not spread uniformly through the wall: they are packed most densely towards the outer surface
9.why: Bài nói sợi KHÔNG phân bố đều mà dày nhất ở mặt ngoài, trái với 'evenly distributed' nên FALSE.

10.quote: many of the traditional houses known as bahareque, which have a bamboo frame covered with a mixture of mud and plaster
10.why: Bài chỉ mô tả cấu tạo nhà bahareque và việc chúng đứng vững sau động đất, không nói kỹ thuật này có nguồn gốc từ châu Á nên NOT GIVEN.

11.quote: One such product, known as strand-woven bamboo, is denser than most hardwoods
11.why: Bài chỉ nói 'denser' (đặc hơn) gỗ cứng, không nói gì về việc khó cắt hơn. Đặc hơn không đồng nghĩa khó cắt hơn nên NOT GIVEN.

12.why: 'some ... environmental advantage is lost in the factory' = quá trình sản xuất làm giảm một phần lợi ích môi trường nên TRUE.

13.why: Bài nói phần lớn kiến trúc sư CHƯA từng được đào tạo, ngược với 'have received some training' nên FALSE.

14.why: Đoạn C mô tả xe thu gom và ống dẫn đưa nodule lên tàu = 'how nodules would be lifted from the seabed to a vessel'.

18.why: Vài milimét mỗi triệu năm = 'how slowly the nodules develop'. Đoạn A. Đoạn D chỉ nói môi trường sống không phục hồi, không nêu tốc độ lớn.

28.why: Tác giả gọi việc gạt bỏ thuyết này những năm 1960 là 'an overreaction' (phản ứng thái quá), trái với 'were right' nên NO.

32.why: Lẩm nhẩm dãy số chiếm nguồn lực ngôn ngữ = 'verbal task' chiếm 'mental capacity'; lợi thế 'disappeared' nên A.

33.quote: whereas Guugu Yimithirr speakers preserved its compass orientation
33.why: 'preserved its compass orientation' = giữ hướng theo la bàn (B). F (trái/phải theo cơ thể) là cách của người Hà Lan.

34.quote: Sceptics such as the psychologist Martin Hale have objected that the two groups differ in more than language: one lives largely in open rural country, the other in towns
34.why: Hale cho rằng hai nhóm khác nhau cả về môi trường sống (nông thôn/thành phố), nên kết quả có thể do môi trường chứ không phải ngôn ngữ (C).

35.quote: when other laboratories attempted to repeat the experiments with larger samples, they found no consistent effect
35.why: 'no consistent effect' = 'failed to find a reliable effect' (D). E là bẫy: chính kết quả gốc, không phải các lần lặp lại, xuất hiện trên tạp chí, sách.

36.quote: Whorf had relied heavily on a single Hopi speaker living in New York
36.why: 'relied heavily on a single Hopi speaker' = 'depended largely on information from one person' (B). C sai: fieldwork sau này bác bỏ ông.

37.quote: these terms are added in a remarkably predictable order
37.why: 'added in a remarkably predictable order' = 'enter languages in a regular sequence' (B). A sai: bài nói các ngôn ngữ khác nhau về số từ chỉ màu.

38.quote: the Pirahã also have a culture in which exact counting plays almost no role in daily life
38.why: Tác giả dè dặt vì văn hóa Pirahã hầu như không cần đếm chính xác, nên không tách được ngôn ngữ và lối sống (C).

39.quote: they tend to appear in tasks that require rapid responses
39.why: 'tasks that require rapid responses' = 'a task has to be done quickly' (B). A ngược lại: khi có thời gian suy nghĩ, khác biệt thu hẹp hoặc biến mất.

40.quote: Because the comparison is made within the same individuals, whose culture and environment stay constant
40.why: So sánh trên cùng một người nên văn hóa và môi trường không đổi = loại bỏ ảnh hưởng của khác biệt văn hóa, môi trường (C).
